title: "Day 2 — Data Structures, Side-by-Side"
subtitle: "Week 1 · vectors & lists vs lists & dicts; `[` `[[` `$` vs `[]` `.loc` `.iloc`"
---

## Cheat sheet (60 seconds)

| Task | R | Python |
|---|---|---|
| 1-D homogeneous container | atomic `vector` `c(1,2,3)` | numpy `array` |
| 1-D heterogeneous container | `list` `list(a=1, b="x")` | `list` / `dict` |
| key → value | named `list` / named `vector` | `dict` |
| table | `data.frame` / `tibble` | pandas `DataFrame` |
| table column | named vector inside a list | `Series` |
| first element | `x[1]` | `x[0]` |
| named pick | `x[["gene"]]`, `x$gene` | `d["gene"]`, `obj.gene` |
| slice positions 2–4 | `x[2:4]` | `x[1:4]` |
| drop position 2 | `x[-2]` | `del`/mask (**`x[-2]` ≠ drop!**) |
| logical filter | `x[x > 3]` | `x[x > 3]` (same idea) |
| count elements | `length(x)` | `len(x)` |
| column names | `names(df)`, `colnames(df)` | `df.columns` |

## Vectors: the atom of R

**Every scalar in R is a vector of length 1.** There is no "plain number"
type — print `2.5` and you get `[1] 2.5`, where `[1]` is the position index.
This is why R functions are written to accept *many* values wherever another
language would demand one, and why vectorization (Pattern 1) is native
rather than bolted on with numpy.

Atomic vectors are *homogeneous* — one type per vector. Mix types and R
silently coerces up the ladder **logical → integer → double → character**
(a classic AI-code surprise):

```{webr}
#| label: coercion
c(1, 2, "three")     # everything became character!
c(TRUE, 1, 0)        # everything became numeric
typeof(c(1L, 2L))    # integer (L suffix) vs double
c(1, NA)             # NA fits in any type — it's "typed missing"
```

```{pyodide}
#| label: coercion-py
[1, 2, "three"]   # fine, stays mixed — lists are heterogeneous by design
```

::: {.callout-tip}
## Why this matters for bioinformatics
A counts matrix that silently became `character` because one cell held
`"-"` is a *real* incident people have spent hours on. `typeof()`,
`str()`, and `table(sapply(df, typeof))` are your first responses to
"the numbers look wrong."
:::

## Attributes: R's metadata side-channels

Any object can carry named attributes — names, dimensions, classes, labels.
`names()` is the attribute you'll touch daily; `attr(x, "...")` is the
generic form:

```{webr}
#| label: attrs
counts <- c(geneA = 120, geneB = 87, geneC = 300)

names(counts)                  # the attribute
counts["geneB"]                # pick by name (keeps the name!)
counts[2] * 2                  # position works too
attributes(counts)             # all attributes at once
```

Python keeps metadata as object fields instead (`arr.dtype`, `df.attrs`,
`Series.name`) — same idea, different flavor: R's attributes live *on* the
data, Python's live *in* the object.

## Lists: R's everything-else

Lists hold anything, including other lists — they're R's dicts *and* objects:

```{webr}
#| label: lists
gene <- list(symbol = "BRCA1", chr = "17", starts = c(1, 5, 9))

gene$symbol          # by name ($ = partial + no spaces)
gene[["chr"]]        # by exact name
gene[["starts"]][2]  # nest in
gene[1]              # ⚠️ returns a LIST containing the element
gene[[1]]            # returns the element itself
length(gene)         # 3 — lists count elements, not contents
```

::: {.callout-important}
## The `[` vs `[[` trap (interview classic)
- `x[1]` → **same container, one element** (a list slice; keeps names)
- `x[[1]]` → **the element itself** ("give me the contents")

Same trap shape in Python: `df[["col"]]` returns a DataFrame,
`df["col"]` returns a Series.
:::

And a shape you'll meet in the wild — lists of lists as "records", exactly
like a JSON response:

```{webr}
#| label: list-json
sample <- list(
  id = "S1",
  metrics = list(reads = 5.2e6, pct_dup = 8.3),
  pass_qc = TRUE
)

sample$metrics$reads            # chain $ through
sample[["metrics"]][["pct_dup"]]
```

```{pyodide}
#| label: list-json-py
sample = {"id": "S1", "metrics": {"reads": 5.2e6, "pct_dup": 8.3}, "pass_qc": True}

print(sample["metrics"]["reads"])
print(sample["metrics"]["pct_dup"])
```

## The full indexing translation table

```{webr}
#| label: r-index
x <- c(10, 20, 30, 40, 50)

x[2]         # 1-based pick
x[2:4]       # slice, END INCLUSIVE
x[-2]        # REMOVE position 2 (negative = exclusion)
x[x > 25]    # logical filter
x[c(1, 5)]   # pick by positions
x[x > 25 & x < 45]   # AND of conditions
```

```{pyodide}
#| label: r-index-py
x = [10, 20, 30, 40, 50]

print(x[1])                     # 0-based pick            -> 20
print(x[1:4])                   # slice, end EXCLUSIVE    -> [20, 30, 40]
del x[1]                        # remove position 1; x is now [10, 30, 40, 50]
print([e for e in x if e > 25]) # logical filter -> [30, 40, 50]
print(x[-2])                    # ⚠️ NOT "drop the 2nd" — it's 2nd from the END -> 40
```

::: {.callout-warning}
## The two traps that bite R↔Python switchers
1. **Negative indices mean opposite things**: R `x[-2]` = "all except the 2nd".
   Python `x[-2]` = "the 2nd from the end".
2. **Slices**: R `2:4` includes position 4. Python `1:4` excludes index 4.
:::

## DataFrames: same idea, different accents

A data.frame **is a list of equal-length vectors** — that's not a metaphor,
call `length(df)` and see. A tibble is a modern data.frame: never coerces
strings to factors, never partial-matches `$`, prints nicely, complains
loudly. A pandas DataFrame is a dict of Series. **All three are "named
columns", just stored differently.**

```{webr}
#| label: df-r
library(tibble)

df <- tibble(
  gene = c("BRCA1", "TP53", "MYC", "EGFR"),
  chr  = c(17, 17, 8, 7),
  expr = c(12.1, 40.3, 3.2, 8.8)
)

df$expr            # column as vector
df[["expr"]]       # same
df[1, ]            # row 1 (note the comma!)
df[, c("gene", "expr")]   # columns by name
df[df$expr > 10, ]        # filter rows by condition
length(df)         # 3 — the columns ARE the list elements
```

```{pyodide}
#| label: df-py
import pandas as pd
df = pd.DataFrame({
  "gene": ["BRCA1", "TP53", "MYC", "EGFR"],
  "chr":  [17, 17, 8, 7],
  "expr": [12.1, 40.3, 3.2, 8.8]})

print(df["expr"], "\n")      # column as Series
print(df.loc[0], "\n")       # row 0 BY LABEL
print(df.iloc[0], "\n")      # row 0 BY POSITION
print(df[["gene", "expr"]], "\n")  # columns by name
print(df[df["expr"] > 10])   # filter rows
```

::: {.callout-tip}
## pandas `.loc` vs `.iloc` — one sentence each
`.loc` = **labels** (row names / names). `.iloc` = **integers** (positions).
R's `df[1, ]` is position- and label-based at once, which is why pandas needs two.
:::

## NA vs NULL vs NaN vs None

| | R | Python/pandas | Meaning |
|---|---|---|---|
| missing value | `NA` | `np.nan`, `pd.NA` | "should be data, isn't" |
| nothing at all | `NULL` | `None` | "no object" |
| bad arithmetic | `NaN` | `nan` | 0/0, sqrt(-1) |

```{webr}
#| label: na-r
v <- c(1, NA, 3)

mean(v)                 # NA spreads!
mean(v, na.rm = TRUE)   # 2
is.na(v)                # where are the NAs?
sum(is.na(v))           # how many
NA == NA                # NA! ("unknown == unknown" is unknown)
v[v == NA]              # ⚠️ never works — use is.na()
```

```{pyodide}
#| label: na-py
import numpy as np, pandas as pd
v = pd.Series([1, np.nan, 3])

print(v.mean())     # pandas SKIPS nan by default (opposite default!)
print(v.isna())     # where are the NAs?
print(v[v.isna()])  # filter to the missing rows
```

::: {.callout-important}
## Default-behavior flip worth memorizing
`mean(na.rm = FALSE)` is R's default — **you** opt out of NAs.
pandas `.mean()` **skips NaN by default** — you opt in.
Silent-source-of-wrong-results #1 in cross-language projects.
:::

## Growing objects: don't

```r
# ❌ AI-smell: quadratic-time growing
out <- c()
for (f in files) out <- c(out, read_one(f))
```

```r
# ✅ collect in a list, bind once
out <- map(files, read_one) |> list_rbind()
```

```{pyodide}
#| label: grow-py
# ✅ same shape in Python: build a list of frames, concat once
import pandas as pd

frames = [pd.DataFrame({"file": [f], "n": [len(f)]}) for f in ["a", "b", "c"]]
out = pd.concat(frames, ignore_index=True)
out
```

## Drills (live pad)

Predict each output **before** running.

```{webr}
#| label: drills
lst <- list(id = "sample_42", reads = c(100, 250, 175), qc = TRUE)
v <- c(5, NA, 12, NA, 3)

# 1. Get "sample_42" two different ways

# 2. Get the SECOND read (250)

# 3. What is lst[2]?  What is lst[[2]]?  Predict, then run.

# 4. Count the NAs in v; mean of v ignoring them

# 5. mtcars: rows where cyl == 6, only mpg and wt (base bracket style)

# 6. Same thing with filter() + select()

# 7. names of the mtcars columns, sorted alphabetically

# 8. typeof(mtcars$cyl) — predict before running

# 9. c(TRUE, TRUE) + c(1, 1) — what type is the result?

# 10. mtcars$mpg[mtcars$mpg > 30] — how many values? (predict, then count)

# 11. Make a named vector of c(2, 3) with names "ctrl", "treated", then
#     look up "treated" by name

# 12. Does lst$qc exist? Does lst$dna? (predict both, no errors allowed)
```

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Expected answers
1. `lst$id` or `lst[["id"]]`
2. `lst$reads[2]`
3. `lst[2]` is a list of length 1 (container); `lst[[2]]` is the numeric vector
4. `sum(is.na(v))` → 2 · `mean(v, na.rm = TRUE)` → 6.667
5. `mtcars[mtcars$cyl == 6, c("mpg", "wt")]`
6. `mtcars |> filter(cyl == 6) |> select(mpg, wt)`
7. `sort(names(mtcars))`
8. `"double"` — data.frame columns are double unless integerized
9. `"numeric"` — logical coerced up the ladder
10. 4 values above 30 (32.4, 30.4, 33.9, 30.4)
11. `setNames(c(2, 3), c("ctrl", "treated"))["treated"]`
12. `lst$qc` → TRUE · `lst$dna` → NULL (no error — $ never errors)
:::

## Python drills (live pad)

Same reflexes, other dialect.

```{pyodide}
#| label: drills-py
d = {"id": "sample_42", "reads": [100, 250, 175], "qc": True}
import pandas as pd

# 1. Get "sample_42" two different ways

# 2. Get the SECOND read

# 3. Slice [100, 250] out of the reads list (one expression)

# 4. What is d[-1]... wait, dicts don't support that. Get the LAST dict KEY
#    (careful: insertion order)

# 5. Build a one-row DataFrame and select the "qc" value with .iloc

# 6. pd.Series([5, None, 12]): count missing, then mean — R vs pandas
#    default behavior: which one needed na.rm?
```

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Expected answers (Python)
1. `d["id"]` or `d.get("id")`
2. `d["reads"][1]` — 0-based!
3. `d["reads"][:2]`
4. `list(d)[-1]` — dicts preserve insertion order (since 3.7)
5. `pd.DataFrame({"qc": [True]}).iloc[0]["qc"]`
6. `s.isna().sum()` → 1 · `s.mean()` → 8.5 **without** any na flag — the flip
:::

## Exercises

### Exercise 1 — predict the type

```{webr}
#| exercise: ex-d2-coerce
# What will typeof() print for each? Write your guess as a comment,
# then run and compare:
typeof(c(1, "a"))
typeof(c(TRUE, FALSE, 1))
typeof(list(1, "a"))
```

::: {.hint exercise="ex-d2-coerce"}
Coercion order: logical → integer → double → character. Lists never coerce.
:::

::: {.solution exercise="ex-d2-coerce"}
```r
typeof(c(1, "a"))           # "character" — 1 was coerced
typeof(c(TRUE, FALSE, 1))   # "double" — TRUE/FALSE became 1/0
typeof(list(1, "a"))        # "list" — no coercion ever
```
:::

### Exercise 2 — negative indexing duel

Same goal in both dialects: **drop** the second element of `c(10, 20, 30)`.

```{webr}
#| exercise: ex-d2-neg
x <- c(10, 20, 30)
# R: one expression, drop the 2nd element
______
```

::: {.hint exercise="ex-d2-neg"}
R: `x[-2]`.
:::

::: {.solution exercise="ex-d2-neg"}
```r
x[-2]        # 10 30
# Python for the same job:  x.pop(1)  or  x[:1] + x[2:]
# Python's x[-2] would return 20 — the second from the END. Total opposite.
```
:::

### Exercise 3 — DataFrame indexing gymnastics

```{webr}
#| exercise: ex-d2-df
library(tibble)
df <- tibble(gene = c("BRCA1", "TP53", "MYC", "EGFR"),
             expr = c(12.1, 40.3, 3.2, 8.8))

# a) expr of TP53 by name (one expression)
# b) the whole ROW of MYC
# c) genes with expr > 10, as a character vector
# d) number of columns of df WITHOUT ncol()
______
```

::: {.hint exercise="ex-d2-df"}
a) `df$expr[df$gene == "TP53"]` · b) `df[df$gene == "MYC", ]` ·
c) `df$gene[df$expr > 10]` · d) `length(df)` — a data.frame is a list of columns!
:::

::: {.solution exercise="ex-d2-df"}
```r
df$expr[df$gene == "TP53"]   # 40.3
df[df$gene == "MYC", ]
df$gene[df$expr > 10]        # "BRCA1" "TP53"
length(df)                   # 2
```
:::

### Exercise 4 — records in the wild

You get a nested list from an API (shape like the `sample` object earlier).
Write `dup_rate(s)` returning `pct_dup / 100` — using `[[` chains, and a
guard that errors clearly if `pass_qc` is FALSE.

```{webr}
#| exercise: ex-d2-nested
sample <- list(id = "S7", metrics = list(reads = 4.1e6, pct_dup = 12.5),
               pass_qc = TRUE)

dup_rate <- function(s) {
  ______
}

dup_rate(sample)
```

::: {.hint exercise="ex-d2-nested"}
Guard: `if (!s$pass_qc) stop("sample failed QC: ", s$id)`. Then
`s$metrics$pct_dup / 100`.
:::

::: {.solution exercise="ex-d2-nested"}
```r
dup_rate <- function(s) {
  if (!s$pass_qc) stop("sample failed QC: ", s$id)
  s$metrics$pct_dup / 100
}
```
:::

### Exercise 5 — NA hygiene

Given `x <- c(3, NA, 7, NA, 2)`: produce (a) the count of NAs, (b) x with
NAs replaced by the mean of the non-missing values (imputation — you'll use
this in scRNA-seq QC constantly), (c) the position of the NAs.

```{webr}
#| exercise: ex-d2-na
x <- c(3, NA, 7, NA, 2)
# a) count
# b) imputed vector
# c) positions
______
```

::: {.hint exercise="ex-d2-na"}
b) `if_else(is.na(x), mean(x, na.rm = TRUE), x)` · c) `which(is.na(x))`
:::

::: {.solution exercise="ex-d2-na"}
```r
sum(is.na(x))                                    # 2
if_else(is.na(x), mean(x, na.rm = TRUE), x)      # 3 4 7 4 2
which(is.na(x))                                  # 2 4
```
:::

### Exercise 6 — the same in Python

```{pyodide}
#| exercise: ex-d2-na-py
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd

s = pd.Series([3, np.nan, 7, np.nan, 2])
# a) count missing
# b) fill NAs with the mean of the rest (one method!)
# c) positions of the NAs (as integer positions)
______

print(s.isna().sum())
print(s.fillna(s.mean()))
print(list(s[s.isna()].index))
```

::: {.hint exercise="ex-d2-na-py"}
`isna().sum()`, `fillna(s.mean())`, `s[s.isna()].index` — pandas has a
dedicated imputation method where R needs `if_else`.
:::

::: {.solution exercise="ex-d2-na-py"}
```python
s.isna().sum()          # 2
s.fillna(s.mean())      # 3.0, 4.0, 7.0, 4.0, 2.0
list(s[s.isna()].index) # [1, 3]
```
:::

## Common pitfalls (real ones)

::: {.callout-warning}
## 1. `$` never errors
`df$exprssion` (typo) silently returns `NULL`, which then flows on and
produces a confusing error three lines later. Tibbles make `$` strict —
one more reason to use them. Quick check: `stopifnot("expr" %in% names(df))`.
:::

::: {.callout-warning}
## 2. `x[x == NA]` returns everything-or-nothing
Comparing to NA gives NA, and NA subsetting returns NA-rows. The only
correct tool is `is.na()`.
:::

::: {.callout-warning}
## 3. Silent type coercion corrupts matrices
One `"-"` in a counts column makes the whole vector character, and
`as.matrix()` of that column is suddenly text. Check `typeof()` after any
import, before any math.
:::

## Self-quiz — predict the output

```{webr}
#| label: quiz
# Q1: length of what?
length(list(a = c(1, 2, 3), b = "x"))

# Q2: what prints?
c("x", 1, TRUE)[3]

# Q3: what prints, and why is it not NA?
y <- c(1, NA); y[is.na(y)] <- 0; y

# Q4: what prints?
d <- data.frame(a = 1:3, b = c("p", "q", "r"))
d$a > 2

# Q5: trap — what happens?
c(1, 2, 3)[-c(1, 3)]
```

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Quiz answers
1. `2` — lists count elements (columns), not contents
2. `"TRUE"` — index 3; everything coerced to character on the way in
3. `1 0` — assigning through `is.na()` replaces the holes; this is the
   idiomatic imputation pattern
4. `FALSE FALSE TRUE` — a logical vector, one value per row
5. `2` — negative *vector* index drops positions 1 AND 3
:::

## Wrap-up checklist

- [ ] `[` keeps the container, `[[` returns contents
- [ ] R negative index = exclude; Python negative index = from the end
- [ ] R slices are inclusive (`2:4`), Python exclusive (`1:4`)
- [ ] `NA` spreads in R math by default; pandas skips it by default
- [ ] Never grow vectors/frames in loops — collect then bind
- [ ] I scored 5/5 on the self-quiz
